chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umeyr, from Hammad, from Al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

He (peace be upon him) was asked about a man who hired a cameleer's camels and sent oil with him to a land, so he claimed that some of the oil skins broke and he spilled what was inside them. He (peace be upon him) said: 'If he wishes, he takes the oil,' and he said: 'He claims it broke, but he is not believed except with a just proof.'

key_terms.اسْتُكْرِيَ: Hired for service (from the root k-r-y, to seek help/service)
key_terms.جَمَّالٍ: Cameleer or carrier (one who transports goods by camel)
key_terms.زِقَاقِ: Skins or containers for oil (plural of ziqqa)
key_terms.يُصَدَّقُ: Is believed/accepted (in a legal testimony context)

ai.seo_question: What is the liability of a hired carrier if goods break during transport?
ai.summary: In this ruling from Imam al-Sadiq (AS), the principle of 'al-gharar' (uncertainty) is applied to commercial contracts, requiring the hired carrier to provide just evidence (bayyina) rather than relying on a mere oath to claim exemption from liability for lost goods. This establishes a high standard of proof in Shia jurisprudence to protect the owner's rights against potential negligence or deceit by the transporter. The hadith underscores the importance of documented accountability in trade, reflecting the broader Islamic legal emphasis on justice (adl) in financial transactions.
